problem_motivation.content: Choosing optimal reactive-element dopants in high-entropy alloys is still empirical because the needed thermodynamic landscape cannot be accessed by first-principles calculations at sufficient compositional resolution.
problem_motivation.evidence_span: Selecting optimal RE dopants in high-entropy alloys remains empirical because the relevant thermodynamic landscape is inaccessible to first-principles at the required compositional resolution.

problem_motivation.content: Predicting oxide-scale adhesion in HEAs is a key challenge for deployment because protective-scale integrity limits long-term performance.
problem_motivation.evidence_span: Understanding and predicting the adhesion of oxide scales to HEA substrates is therefore a central challenge for the deployment of these materials.

problem_motivation.content: Reactive-element selection for specific alloy-oxide pairs remains empirical.
problem_motivation.evidence_span: Despite decades of research, RE selection for a given alloy–oxide combination remains largely empirical.

problem_motivation.content: The design space is too large for exhaustive experiments.
problem_motivation.evidence_span: With six principal elements, five RE candidates, two oxide types, and continuous composition ranges, the design space is inaccessible to exhaustive experimental exploration.

problem_motivation.content: The observation of near-zero or positive sulfur segregation in some Al- and Mn-containing alloys motivates constructing a sulfur-immunity phase diagram.
problem_motivation.evidence_span: The observation that certain Al- and Mn-containing alloys exhibit near- zero or positive S segregation enthalpies motivates the construction of a sulfur immunity phase diagram.

prior_approach.content: Prior experimental studies established oxidation behavior in CoCrFeMnNi-based HEAs.
prior_approach.evidence_span: Extensive experimental work has established the oxidation phenomenology of key HEA families.

prior_approach.content: Laplanche et al. studied oxidation in the Cantor system and identified Mn-rich oxides and Mn-diffusion-controlled oxidation.
prior_approach.evidence_span: For the CoCrFeMnNi (Cantor) system, Laplanche et al. [9] showed that Mn-rich oxides (α-Mn2O3 at 600–800◦C, Mn3O4 at 900◦C) dominate the scale, with an oxidation activation energy of 130 ± 10 kJ/mol controlled by Mn diffusion through the oxide rather than sluggish diffusion in the alloy matrix [10].

prior_approach.content: Dehury et al. examined long-term oxidation of related HEAs at 1000°C.
prior_approach.evidence_span: Dehury et al. [11] extended these observations to 30-day exposures at 1000◦C, demonstrating that Mn-free CoCrFeNi forms a more continuous, better-adherent oxide with an oxidation rate constant one order of magnitude lower than that of the Cantor alloy, while Cr-free CoFeMnNi undergoes catastrophic oxidation with phase decomposition.

prior_approach.content: Holcomb et al. compared scale retention across CoCrFeMnNi variants.
prior_approach.evidence_span: Holcomb et al. [7] confirmed this hierarchy across eight CoCrFeMnNi variants, finding that low-Mn, high-Cr compositions exhibited the best scale retention.

prior_approach.content: Butler and Weaver showed Al additions promote protective alumina formation.
prior_approach.evidence_span: For Al-containing systems, Butler and Weaver [12] showed that ≥20 at% Al promotes continuous protective Al2O3

prior_approach.content: Lu et al. showed Y and Hf co-doping improves alumina scale formation.
prior_approach.evidence_span: while Lu et al. [4] demonstrated that co-doping AlCoCrFeNi with only 0.02 at% each of Y and Hf produces a uniform α-Al2O3 scale just 4.6 µm thick after 1000 h at 1100◦C.

prior_approach.content: Reviews concluded Al and Cr are key for protective oxide formation, while Mn is detrimental.
prior_approach.evidence_span: Comprehensive reviews [13] have concluded that Al and Cr are the most important elements for protective oxide formation, while Mn degrades oxidation resistance through porous, poorly adhering scale phases.

prior_approach.content: Prior work documented sulfur-induced adhesion loss in superalloys and HEAs.
prior_approach.evidence_span: as documented in Ni-based superalloys [18, 19] and increasingly in HEA systems [5, 7].

prior_approach.content: Chen et al. studied selective oxidation effects in Al0.1CrCoFeNi.
prior_approach.evidence_span: Chen et al. [24] further demonstrated that selective oxidation of Cr, Co, and Fe in Al0.1CrCoFeNi creates a Ni-enriched subsurface layer that hinders repassivation

prior_approach.content: First-principles DFT has been used to study specific systems.
prior_approach.evidence_span: First-principles density functional theory has provided valuable atomistic insight for specific systems [25–28]

prior_approach.content: The authors previously extended the macroscopic atom model to multicomponent alloys and validated it against DFT.
prior_approach.evidence_span: In our previous paper [29], we extended the macroscopic atom model (MAM) [30, 31] to multicomponent alloys, where we validated the framework against DFT for CoCrFeNi and AlCoCrFeNi systems.

prior_approach.content: Prior experiments by Laplanche et al. reported scale spallation in the Cantor alloy during isothermal oxidation.
prior_approach.evidence_span: Laplanche et al. [9] reported scale spallation during isothermal oxidation of the Cantor alloy, manifested as small weight losses in TGA curves.

prior_approach.content: Prior experiments by Dehury et al. compared oxidation behavior of CoCrFeNi and CoCrFeMnNi after long-term high-temperature exposure.
prior_approach.evidence_span: More directly, Dehury et al. [11] found that after 30 days at 1000◦C, CoCrFeNi formed a relatively continuous oxide layer with good surface adherence, whereas CoCrFeMnNi exhibited a rough, discontinuous, and significantly spalled scale with Kirkendall pores at the metal–oxide interface.

prior_approach.content: Lu et al. experimentally used Y/Hf co-doping in alumina-forming AlCoCrFeNi.
prior_approach.evidence_span: Lu et al. [4] achieved exceptional oxidation resistance in Y/Hf co-doped AlCoCrFeNi, an alumina-forming alloy

prior_approach.content: Previous DFT work showed Ni sites are most unfavorable for RE segregation.

prior_approach.content: Dehury et al. performed vacuum-annealing experiments to study Mn migration.
prior_approach.evidence_span: Dehury et al. [11] provided direct experimental evidence for this duality. Their vacuum-annealing experiment at 1000◦C confirmed that Mn migration to the surface is oxidation-driven rather than thermally driven

prior_approach.content: Veselkov et al. reviewed oxidation-resistant HEAs and recommended AlCoCrFeNi alloys with refractory additions.
prior_approach.evidence_span: The review by Veselkov et al. [13] concluded that AlCoCrFeNi alloys with additions of refractory elements represent the most promising direction for oxidation-resistant HEAs

prior_approach.content: Chen et al. showed analogous selective oxidation effects during aqueous corrosion in Al0.1CrCoFeNi.
prior_approach.evidence_span: Chen et al. [24] showed that selective oxidation in Al0.1CrCoFeNi during corrosion alters the subsurface composition in a manner analogous to high-temperature oxidation

prior_limitation.evidence_span: but the computational cost of interface supercell calculations limits coverage to isolated configurations.

inspiration_source.content: The Cr-adhesion trend is interpreted by analogy to the percolation threshold for passive-film formation reported by Xie et al.
inspiration_source.evidence_span: The dominance of Cr as the adhesion lever at Cr2O3 connects to the percolation threshold concept. Xie et al. [41] showed that a minimum of ∼10–12 at% Cr is required for continuous passive film formation in Fe–Cr and Ni–Cr systems.

causal_claim.content: Segregation enthalpy difference governs the universal exponential collapse of crossover concentrations.
causal_claim.evidence_span: All crossover concentrations collapse onto a universal exponential governed by the segregation enthalpy difference, providing a transferable design rule.

causal_claim.content: Mn-free CoCrFeNi yields a more continuous, better-adherent oxide and lower oxidation rate than the Cantor alloy.
causal_claim.evidence_span: demonstrating that Mn-free CoCrFeNi forms a more continuous, better-adherent oxide with an oxidation rate constant one order of magnitude lower than that of the Cantor alloy

causal_claim.content: Cr-free CoFeMnNi causes catastrophic oxidation with phase decomposition.
causal_claim.evidence_span: while Cr-free CoFeMnNi undergoes catastrophic oxidation with phase decomposition.

causal_claim.content: Low-Mn, high-Cr composition improves scale retention.
causal_claim.evidence_span: finding that low-Mn, high-Cr compositions exhibited the best scale retention.

causal_claim.content: At least 20 at% Al promotes continuous protective Al2O3.
causal_claim.evidence_span: ≥20 at% Al promotes continuous protective Al2O3

causal_claim.content: Trace Y and Hf co-doping produces a uniform thin α-Al2O3 scale.
causal_claim.evidence_span: co-doping AlCoCrFeNi with only 0.02 at% each of Y and Hf produces a uniform α-Al2O3 scale just 4.6 µm thick after 1000 h at 1100◦C.

causal_claim.content: Mn degrades oxidation resistance by forming porous, poorly adhering scales.
causal_claim.evidence_span: Mn degrades oxidation resistance through porous, poorly adhering scale phases.

causal_claim.content: Sulfur accumulation at oxide-metal interfaces weakens adhesion and promotes spallation.
causal_claim.evidence_span: Sulfur at bulk concentrations below 30 ppm can accumulate at oxide–metal interfaces to levels sufficient to weaken adhesion and promote spallation [16, 17]

causal_claim.content: Reactive-element additions counteract sulfur effects via interfacial displacement, oxide-growth modification, and RE-O peg formation.
causal_claim.evidence_span: The addition of REs such as Hf and Y at trace levels counteracts sulfur through competitive interfacial displacement, modification of oxide growth kinetics, and formation of stable RE–O pegs that anchor the scale [14, 20–23].

causal_claim.content: Selective oxidation of Cr, Co, and Fe creates a Ni-enriched subsurface layer that hinders repassivation.
causal_claim.evidence_span: selective oxidation of Cr, Co, and Fe in Al0.1CrCoFeNi creates a Ni-enriched subsurface layer that hinders repassivation

causal_claim.content: Because the oxide-energy error is a constant offset for a given oxide, comparative rankings and related metrics are unaffected.
causal_claim.evidence_span: Since this enters Wsep as a constant additive offset for all alloys at a given oxide, all inter-alloy rankings, ∆Wsep enhancements, segregation enthalpies, and crossover concentrations are unaffected

causal_claim.content: Validation against DFT supports using MAM as a reliable basis for comparative screening.
causal_claim.evidence_span: validation against DFT [29] demonstrates that the MAM correctly reproduces segregation hierarchies and adhesion trends, providing a reliable basis for comparative screening.

causal_claim.content: Al-containing alloys have lower surface energies because Al has lower surface enthalpy.
causal_claim.evidence_span: Al-containing alloys consistently exhibit lower surface energies by 0.2–0.3 J/m2, reflecting the low surface enthalpy of Al (76 kJ/mol) compared to Co (127), Cr (121), Fe (129), Ni (121), and Mn (85 kJ/mol) [31].

causal_claim.content: Mn lowers surface energy relative to CoCrFeNi because Mn has lower surface enthalpy.
causal_claim.evidence_span: Within each group, Mn-containing variants show intermediate values; for example, the Cantor alloy (2.28 J/m2) lies below CoCrFeNi (2.46 J/m2) due to Mn’s lower surface enthalpy.

causal_claim.content: Cross-interface chemical interactions dominate adhesion differences more than surface energies because surface-energy contributions partially cancel.
causal_claim.evidence_span: Because the alloy surface energy enters both the numerator of Wsep and the interfacial energy term with partially canceling contributions, the cross-interface chemical interactions, rather than the surface energies themselves, emerge as the dominant factor differentiating adhesion across families

causal_claim.content: Chromia's adhesion advantage comes from stronger Cr–O cross-interface bonding.
causal_claim.evidence_span: This systematic advantage arises primarily from the stronger Cr–O cross-interface bonding (∆H◦= −578 kJ/mol) relative to the Al–O interactions already present within the alumina lattice

causal_claim.content: Adding Al slightly increases Wsep at Cr2O3 through strong Al–Cr interaction.
causal_claim.evidence_span: First, Al increases Wsep at Cr2O3 (CoCrFeNi: 5.90 →AlCoCrFeNi: 5.93 J/m2) through the strong Al–Cr interaction (∆H◦ AlCr = −87 kJ/mol)

causal_claim.content: Adding Al decreases Wsep at Al2O3 because like-element contacts across the interface do not contribute chemical bonding.
causal_claim.evidence_span: while decreasing it at Al2O3 (5.46 →5.36 J/m2) because like-element contacts across the interface contribute nothing to the chemical bonding.

causal_claim.content: Mn systematically reduces adhesion at both chromia and alumina interfaces.
causal_claim.evidence_span: Second, Mn systematically reduces Wsep at both interfaces: CoCrFeNi (5.90) → Cantor (5.82 J/m2), and AlCoCrFeNi (5.93) →AlCoCrFeMnNi (5.87 J/m2).

causal_claim.content: Rapid outward Mn diffusion creates Kirkendall porosity and further weakens adhesion by void-mediated decohesion.
causal_claim.evidence_span: The rapid outward Mn diffusion creates Kirkendall porosity [11], further weakening adhesion through mechanical void-mediated decohesion, thereby amplifying the thermodynamic weakness predicted here.

causal_claim.content: Y ranks second because weaker Y–O interaction is partly offset by more favorable matrix interactions.
causal_claim.evidence_span: although the Y–O interaction (−953 kJ/mol) is weaker than Hf–O (−1113 kJ/mol), Y’s more favorable matrix interactions partially compensate, placing it second.

causal_claim.content: La ranks fourth because its large molar volume causes an unfavorable mismatch contribution.
causal_claim.evidence_span: La ranks fourth because its large molar volume (VLa = 22.55 cm3/mol) creates an unfavorable mismatch contribution.

causal_claim.content: The ranking inversion originates in Term 1 because La interacts more strongly with Al-dominated oxide than Hf does at Al2O3, while the reverse holds at Cr2O3.
causal_claim.evidence_span: The inversion originates in Term 1: La’s interaction with the Al-dominated oxide (−1.52 eV) exceeds that of Hf (−1.38 eV) at Al2O3, driven by the more exothermic La–Al interaction (∆H◦ LaAl = −231 kJ/mol vs. Hf–Al: −215 kJ/mol), while the reverse holds at Cr2O3 (∆H◦ LaCr = +93 kJ/mol).

causal_claim.content: La's mismatch penalty is not large enough to undo its advantage at Al2O3.
causal_claim.evidence_span: The mismatch penalty for La (Term 4: +0.24 eV) is constant across oxide types and insufficient to reverse the ranking at Al2O3.

causal_claim.content: Ti's favorable matrix interactions reduce its net segregation driving force despite strong Ti–O interaction.
causal_claim.evidence_span: Despite having a substantial Ti–O interaction (−945 kJ/mol), Ti’s favorable matrix interactions reduce the net segregation driving force

causal_claim.content: All families lose adhesion monotonically as sulfur concentration increases, but sensitivity differs by composition.
causal_claim.evidence_span: All families show monotonic adhesion decline with increasing S concentration, but the rate and magnitude of decline differ substantially.

causal_claim.content: Al-containing alloys are less sulfur-sensitive because weaker S segregation means less interfacial sulfur and less bond-network disruption.
causal_claim.evidence_span: This reduced sensitivity of Al-containing alloys correlates with their weaker S segregation enthalpies: less S reaches the interface at equilibrium, and the interfacial bonding network is less disrupted per unit of S coverage.

causal_claim.content: Despite steep sulfur sensitivity, CoCrFeMn needs very little RE to block sulfur because it has the lowest RE/S crossover concentrations.
causal_claim.evidence_span: However, as shown later in this section and in Section 3.5, this system also has the lowest crossover concentrations for RE displacement of S, meaning that in practice, very little RE is needed to prevent S from reaching the interface.

causal_claim.content: Typical RE additions exceed thermodynamic minimums by 2–3 orders of magnitude because extra RE compensates kinetic limitations and sequestration.
causal_claim.evidence_span: Since typical RE alloying additions are 0.05–0.5 wt% (50–5000 ppm atomic), this confirms that practical RE levels exceed the thermodynamic minimum by 2–3 orders of magnitude. The excess serves primarily to compensate for kinetic limitations including slow bulk diffusion of RE to the interface, consumption by internal oxidation, and RE sequestration at grain boundaries [14, 15].

causal_claim.content: Removing Ni lowers RE crossover concentrations because Ni competes with REs for interfacial sites.
causal_claim.evidence_span: The absence of Ni, which competes with REs for interfacial sites, removes a key impediment to RE segregation.

causal_claim.content: La has a practical advantage at Al2O3: much less La than Hf is needed for equivalent protection.
causal_claim.evidence_span: The practical implication is stark: 0.02 ppm La provides the same interfacial protection at Al2O3 as 0.11 ppm Hf, a 5× advantage.

causal_claim.content: CoCrFeMn is easiest to protect because strong Mn–S bulk interaction weakens sulfur segregation while Hf still segregates strongly to the interface.
causal_claim.evidence_span: CoCrFeMn is the easiest alloy to protect because its strong Mn–S bulk interaction weakens S segregation (∆HS seg = −0.22 eV), while Hf maintains strong interfacial segregation (−1.01 eV).

causal_claim.content: Hardest-case crossover is high because CoCrFeNi strongly segregates sulfur and Ti has only a small segregation advantage over sulfur.
causal_claim.evidence_span: CoCrFeNi has the strongest S segregation among all families (−0.46 eV at Cr2O3), and Ti’s relatively weak segregation (−0.80 eV) provides the smallest thermodynamic advantage over S.

causal_claim.content: Crossover concentration increases with temperature because higher temperature reduces Boltzmann selectivity between RE and S.
causal_claim.evidence_span: The crossover concentrations increase monotonically with temperature, as expected from Eq. (5), where higher temperatures reduce the Boltzmann selectivity between RE and S.

causal_claim.content: Higher Cr content increases adhesion at Cr2O3.
causal_claim.evidence_span: Wsep at Cr2O3 increases monotonically with Cr content, with increasing Cr from 10 to 35 at% rais- ing adhesion by approximately 0.3 J/m2.

causal_claim.content: Trace-RE separability allows base-composition optimization and RE selection to be done independently.
causal_claim.evidence_span: This separability means that alloy designers can first optimize the base composition for adhesion, then independently select the RE.

causal_claim.content: The best-segregating element is not necessarily the best interfacial strengthener.
causal_claim.evidence_span: The element that segregates most readily is not necessarily the one that strengthens the interface most.

causal_claim.content: Near-zero sulfur segregation in Al-containing alloys inflates η at Cr2O3 because the denominator becomes very small.
causal_claim.evidence_span: The Al-containing alloys at Cr2O3 exhibit elevated η values because their near-zero S segregation in the denominator amplifies the index

causal_claim.content: RE effects are stronger for chromia formers than for alumina formers.
causal_claim.evidence_span: Consistent with the findings of Hou and Stringer [22], the RE effect exerts a stronger influence on chromia formers than on their alumina-forming counterparts.

causal_claim.content: Increasing Mn lowers adhesion at both interfaces by about 0.1 J/m2.
causal_claim.evidence_span: Increasing Mn from 0 to 30 at% reduces Wsep by approximately 0.1 J/m2 at both interfaces

causal_claim.content: Mn both weakens oxide-metal bonding and protects against sulfur poisoning.
causal_claim.evidence_span: Mn thus presents a double-edged character where it weakens the oxide–metal bond while simultaneously protecting the interface from S poi- soning.

causal_claim.content: Whether Mn is beneficial depends on sulfur level: harmful in ultra-low-S alloys, but potentially compensating in typical industrial alloys.
causal_claim.evidence_span: For ultra-low-S alloys (<5 ppm), the adhesion penalty dominates, and Mn is detrimental. For typical industrial alloys with 10–50 ppm S, the S-gettering effect may partially or fully compensate.

causal_claim.content: Mn does not materially block the RE effect, so intrinsic sulfur resistance and RE-enhanced adhesion can coexist.
causal_claim.evidence_span: indicating that Mn does not impede the RE effect. The benefits of intrinsic S resistance and RE- mediated adhesion enhancement can coexist

causal_claim.content: Complexity across alloy composition, RE, and oxide reduces to a single thermodynamic parameter.
causal_claim.evidence_span: The entire complexity of alloy composition, RE choice, and oxide type reduces to a single thermodynamic parameter.

causal_claim.content: Knowing RE and sulfur segregation enthalpies lets designers read off minimum RE concentration from the universal curve.
causal_claim.evidence_span: The practical consequence is that an alloy designer who knows ∆HRE seg and ∆HS seg for any system obtainable from a seconds-long MAM calculation can read the minimum RE concentration directly from the universal curve.

causal_claim.content: This composition achieves strong adhesion without RE additions through intrinsic resistance to sulfur segregation.
causal_claim.evidence_span: This com- position achieves strong adhesion without any RE addition, entirely through intrinsic thermodynamic resistance to S segregation.

causal_claim.content: High adhesion corresponds to compact, continuous scales with smooth interfaces because strong bonding resists delamination and preserves contact during growth.
causal_claim.evidence_span: High-Wsep alloys (CoCrFeNi, AlCoCrFeNi at Cr2O3) form compact, contin- uous oxide scales with smooth metal–oxide interfaces [4, 11], because strong bonding resists delamination and maintains intimate contact during growth.

causal_claim.content: Low adhesion corresponds to porous, fragmented, spalled scales with voids.
causal_claim.evidence_span: Low-Wsep alloys (Mn-rich compositions, Cr-free alloys) develop porous, frag- mented scales with evidence of spallation and void formation [7, 9, 11].

causal_claim.content: The combination of weak intrinsic adhesion and void-induced contact loss explains severe spallation in the Cantor alloy.
causal_claim.evidence_span: The combination of lower intrinsic adhesion and void-mediated area reduction explains the severe spallation observed in the Cantor alloy.

causal_claim.content: Preferential oxidation of Cr, Co, and Fe leaves a Ni-rich subsurface that hinders repassivation.
causal_claim.evidence_span: Cr, Co, and Fe preferentially oxidize, leaving a Ni-rich subsurface that hinders repassivation.

mechanism_principle.content: Interplay between RE-O and RE-matrix interaction enthalpies explains the oxide-dependent ranking inversion.
mechanism_principle.evidence_span: driven by the interplay between RE–O and RE–matrix interaction enthalpies

mechanism_principle.content: The segregation enthalpy difference is the governing principle behind the universal exponential behavior of crossover concentrations.
mechanism_principle.evidence_span: governed by the segregation enthalpy difference

mechanism_principle.content: Oxide-scale adhesion is governed by oxide-metal interfacial chemistry and segregation of impurities/dopants.
mechanism_principle.evidence_span: Scale adhesion is controlled by the chemistry of the oxide–metal interface, governed by the segregation of trace impurities and dopants [14, 15].

mechanism_principle.content: REs mitigate sulfur by displacement at the interface, changing oxide growth kinetics, and forming stable anchoring RE-O pegs.
mechanism_principle.evidence_span: through competitive interfacial displacement, modification of oxide growth kinetics, and formation of stable RE–O pegs that anchor the scale

mechanism_principle.content: Compositional changes at the interface directly control protective-film integrity.
mechanism_principle.evidence_span: showing how compositional changes at the interface directly control the integrity of the protective film.

mechanism_principle.content: Preferential Al surface enrichment explains the lower surface energy trend.
mechanism_principle.evidence_span: This trend is consistent with the predicted preferential surface enrichment of Al by the Gibbs adsorption isotherm.

mechanism_principle.content: The Mn adhesion penalty comes from weaker Mn–O interactions than competing metal–O interactions.
mechanism_principle.evidence_span: This reduction of 0.06–0.08 J/m2 arises from the weaker Mn–O interaction (−520 kJ/mol) relative to Cr–O (−578), Co–O (−302), and Fe–O (−413 kJ/mol).

mechanism_principle.content: Model explains Mn effect via weaker Mn–O bonds, while experiments show fast Mn outward diffusion and Mn-rich outer-layer growth.
mechanism_principle.evidence_span: The model attributes the adhesion reduction to weaker Mn–O cross-interface bonds, while experiments show that Mn diffuses outward through the oxide faster than any other element [7, 9, 11], forming a Mn-rich outer layer whose growth rate exceeds that of the parent alloy by an order of magnitude.

mechanism_principle.content: Cr2O3 ranking reflects a balance between solute–oxide attraction and solute–bulk penalty.
mechanism_principle.evidence_span: This ordering reflects the balance between the solute–oxide attraction (Term 1) and the solute–bulk penalty (Term 3)

mechanism_principle.content: Adhesion enhancement is governed by RE–O interaction strength at the interface, not just segregation tendency.
mechanism_principle.evidence_span: This distinction arises because ∆Wsep depends on the RE–O interaction enthalpy once the RE reaches the interface (Hf–O: −1113 kJ/mol > Zr–O: −1098 > Y–O: −953 kJ/mol), not on the thermo- dynamic driving force for getting there.

mechanism_principle.content: The proposed index measures both out-segregation versus sulfur and bond strengthening versus the matrix average.
mechanism_principle.evidence_span: The first ratio measures how much more strongly the RE segregates than S; the second measures how much stronger the RE–O bond is relative to the average matrix–O bond it replaces.

mechanism_principle.content: High η in Al-containing alloys reflects low need for RE protection because sulfur protection is already intrinsic.
mechanism_principle.evidence_span: reflecting the physical reality that these alloys require minimal RE intervention for S protection.

mechanism_principle.content: Mn lowers adhesion by diluting stronger metal–oxygen bonds with weaker Mn–O bonding.
mechanism_principle.evidence_span: reflecting the dilution of stronger metal–O bonds by the weaker Mn–O interaction.

mechanism_principle.content: Strong Mn–S interaction traps sulfur in the bulk and discourages interfacial segregation.
mechanism_principle.evidence_span: The physical origin is the Mn–S interaction enthalpy (∆H◦ MnS = −225 kJ/- mol), which is more exothermic than Ni–S (−135), Co–S (−153), or Cr–S (−183 kJ/mol). This strong Mn–S bulk interaction creates a thermodynamic trap that stabilizes S in the alloy matrix and penalizes its migration to the interface.

mechanism_principle.content: Oxidation drives Mn outward diffusion via favorable Mn–O interaction, but weak Mn–O interfacial bonding leaves the scale poorly anchored.
mechanism_principle.evidence_span: The present thermodynamic analysis explains why: the Mn–O interaction provides the driving force for outward diffusion, while the weak Mn–O bond at the interface ensures that the resulting scale is poorly anchored.

mechanism_principle.content: The sulfur-immunity threshold comes from combined sulfur trapping by Al and Mn, whose sulfide interactions are more exothermic than those of Ni, Co, or Cr.
mechanism_principle.evidence_span: This threshold arises from the combined S-trapping effect of Al (∆H◦ AlS = −363 kJ/mol) and Mn (∆H◦ MnS = −225 kJ/mol), both more exothermic than the Ni–S, Co–S, or Cr–S interactions.

mechanism_principle.content: High Al content both traps sulfur in the bulk and improves interfacial bonding via favorable Al–O interactions.
mechanism_principle.evidence_span: The high Al content cre- ates both a strong Al–S bulk trap and favorable Al–O cross-interface bonding.

mechanism_principle.content: Kirkendall pores from outward Mn diffusion reduce contact area and further lower practical adhesion below thermodynamic Wsep.
mechanism_principle.evidence_span: Vacancy condensation from preferential outward Mn diffusion creates voids that re- duce the effective contact area, further decreasing practical adhesion below the thermodynamic Wsep.

hypothesis_statement.content: This work applies the validated MAM framework to screen adhesion and rank reactive elements across CoCrFeMnNiAl sub-families and oxide interfaces.
hypothesis_statement.evidence_span: Here we apply this framework to screen adhesion across nine sub-families of the CoCrFeMnNiAl system at both Cr2O3 and Al2O3 interfaces, ranking five REs for segregation tendency, adhesion enhancement, and sulfur displacement, and systematically comparing the predictions with the experimental oxidation literature.

hypothesis_statement.content: The model is intended for relative comparisons rather than absolute adhesion energies.
hypothesis_statement.evidence_span: the model’s predictive strength therefore lies in relative comparisons rather than absolute adhesion energies.

hypothesis_statement.content: Design implication: choose Hf for chromia-forming alloys and La or Y for alumina-forming alloys.
hypothesis_statement.evidence_span: Hf should be preferred for chromia-forming alloys, while La or Y should be preferred for alumina-forming compositions.

hypothesis_statement.content: La alone may provide even stronger interfacial enrichment at Al2O3 than Y/Hf.
hypothesis_statement.evidence_span: However, the model suggests that La alone could have provided even stronger interfacial enrichment at Al2O3 (−1.29 eV), a prediction that warrants experimental verification.

hypothesis_statement.content: Ni-free chromia-forming HEAs may need much lower RE additions for similar protection.
hypothesis_statement.evidence_span: This prediction identifies Ni-free chromia-forming HEAs that may require substantially lower RE additions for equivalent interfacial protection.

hypothesis_statement.content: The authors define an RE protection window as the temperature range where bulk RE concentration exceeds crossover concentration.
hypothesis_statement.evidence_span: These curves define the RE protection window: the temperature range over which a given RE bulk concentration exceeds the crossover threshold.

hypothesis_statement.content: Non-equiatomic, Cr-rich variants should improve adhesion substantially.
hypothesis_statement.evidence_span: indicating that non-equiatomic, Cr-rich vari- ants could provide substantial adhesion improvements.

hypothesis_statement.content: The authors propose a single composite RE-effectiveness index combining segregation and bonding.
hypothesis_statement.evidence_span: To provide a single-metric ranking, we define a dimensionless composite RE effectiveness index that combines both:

hypothesis_statement.content: The sulfur-vulnerability map is experimentally testable by interfacial sulfur measurements across the predicted boundary.
hypothesis_statement.evidence_span: This map constitutes, to our knowledge, the first thermodynamic phase diagram for sulfur vulnerability in HEAs and is directly testable by SIMS or AES measurements of interfacial S concentration in alloys positioned on opposite sides of the boundary.

hypothesis_statement.content: All crossover concentrations should collapse onto one master curve when plotted against the segregation-enthalpy difference.
hypothesis_statement.evidence_span: Eq. (5) predicts that all crossover con- centrations should collapse onto a single master curve when plotted against the segregation enthalpy difference ∆∆H = ∆HRE seg.

hypothesis_statement.content: The authors pose an inverse-design question of which composition maximizes adhesion while remaining sulfur-immune.
hypothesis_statement.evidence_span: The natural convergence of the S immunity boundary and the adhesion maps raises the question: what composition simultaneously achieves S im- munity and maximum adhesion?

hypothesis_statement.content: Moderately elevated Al plus some Mn may achieve sulfur immunity while retaining an FCC-based structure.
hypothesis_statement.evidence_span: Non-equiatomic variants with moderately elevated Al (15–25 at%) combined with 10–15 at% Mn could potentially achieve S immunity while maintaining an FCC-based structure.

evidence_result.content: Screening found an oxide-dependent inversion: Hf ranks best at Cr2O3 while La ranks best at Al2O3.
evidence_result.evidence_span: The screening reveals an oxide-dependent ranking inversion, with Hf dominating at Cr2O3 and La dominating at Al2O3

evidence_result.content: Mn-containing alloys were found to have intrinsic sulfur resistance.
evidence_result.evidence_span: Mn-containing alloys exhibit intrinsic sulfur resistance, consistent with their experimentally observed oxidation characteristics.

evidence_result.content: A phase diagram shows that compositions with Al + Mn above about 25 at% are thermodynamically immune to sulfur-induced adhesion loss.
evidence_result.evidence_span: A sulfur immunity phase diagram identifies compositions with Al + Mn ≳25 at% as thermodynamically immune to S-induced adhesion loss.

evidence_result.content: Inverse design identified Co16Cr16Fe16Ni16Al35 as the best sulfur-immune composition without reactive-element doping, with Wsep of 5.95 J/m2.
evidence_result.evidence_span: Inverse design identifies Co16Cr16Fe16Ni16Al35 as the optimal S-immune composition with Wsep = 5.95 J/m2 without RE doping.

evidence_result.content: Prior validation against DFT showed MAM reproduces segregation hierarchies and adhesion trends.
evidence_result.evidence_span: Despite these approximations, validation against DFT [29] demonstrates that the MAM correctly reproduces segregation hierarchies and adhesion trends, providing a reliable basis for comparative screening.

evidence_result.content: The full screening of more than 500 calculations finished in under 3 minutes on one CPU core.
evidence_result.evidence_span: The entire screening comprising over 500 individual calculations completed in under 3 minutes on a single processor core.

evidence_result.content: Computed surface energies span 1.97–2.46 J/m2, separating Al-containing from Al-free alloys.
evidence_result.evidence_span: The computed alloy surface energies range from 1.97 J/m2 (AlCoCrMnNi) to 2.46 J/m2 (CoCrFeNi), with a clear dichotomy between Al-containing and Al-free compositions (Fig. 1).

evidence_result.content: Predicted CoCrFeNi surface energy matches DFT values.
evidence_result.evidence_span: The predicted value for CoCrFeNi agrees well with DFT calculations reporting 2.3–2.6 J/m2 depending on crystallographic orientation [39].

evidence_result.content: Chromia interfaces consistently have higher adhesion than alumina across all compositions.
evidence_result.evidence_span: Chromia interfaces consistently produce higher Wsep than alumina across all alloy compositions (Fig. 2), with differences ranging from 0.43 J/m2 (Cantor) to 0.60 J/m2 (AlCrFeNi).

evidence_result.content: Experimental literature reports better adhesion for chromia-forming alloys under moderate oxidation.
evidence_result.evidence_span: consistent with the experimental observation that chromia-forming alloys tend to exhibit superior scale adhesion under moderate oxidation conditions [21, 22].

evidence_result.content: Experiments showed CoCrFeNi had better scale continuity and adherence than CoCrFeMnNi, which showed spallation and Kirkendall pores.
evidence_result.evidence_span: after 30 days at 1000◦C, CoCrFeNi formed a relatively continuous oxide layer with good surface adherence, whereas CoCrFeMnNi exhibited a rough, discontinuous, and significantly spalled scale with Kirkendall pores at the metal–oxide interface.

evidence_result.content: Measured oxidation rate constant was about seven times lower for CoCrFeNi than CoCrFeMnNi.
evidence_result.evidence_span: Their measured oxidation rate constant for CoCrFeNi (8.8 × 10−5 (mg/mm2)3/s) was approximately seven times lower than for CoCrFeMnNi (59 × 10−5 (mg/mm2)3/s).

evidence_result.content: Predicted adhesion hierarchy matches experimental rankings.
evidence_result.evidence_span: The adhesion hierarchy predicted here, CoCrFeNi > CoCrFeMnNi ≫CoFeMnNi, matches the experimental rankings at Cr2O3 maps.

evidence_result.content: At Cr2O3, RE segregation ranking is consistently Hf > Y ≈ Zr > La > Ti across all families.
evidence_result.evidence_span: At the Cr2O3 interface, the ranking is remarkably consistent across all families: Hf > Y ≈Zr > La > Ti.

evidence_result.content: At Al2O3, segregation ranking inverts and La becomes strongest in most families.
evidence_result.evidence_span: At the Al2O3 interface, a dramatic ranking inversion occurs: La becomes the strongest segregant in most families, with Y second.

evidence_result.content: This prior experiment indirectly supports the prediction that Y and Hf are effective at Al2O3.
evidence_result.evidence_span: consistent with our prediction that both Y and Hf are effective at Al2O3, with segregation enthalpies of −1.15 and −1.07 eV respectively.

evidence_result.content: Ti is the weakest segregant across all systems.
evidence_result.evidence_span: Ti consistently ranks weakest across all systems, with segregation enthalpies 30–50% below the strongest segregant.

evidence_result.evidence_span: CoCrFeNi and the Cantor alloy lose approximately 0.35 J/m2 of adhesion at 10 at% S surface fraction at Cr2O3, while AlCoCrFeNi loses only 0.20 J/m2.

evidence_result.content: CoCrFeMn has the steepest Wsep decline per unit sulfur at Cr2O3.
evidence_result.evidence_span: The CoCrFeMn system shows the steepest decline in Wsep per unit S at Cr2O3

evidence_result.content: Crossover concentrations for RE displacement of sulfur span over two orders of magnitude.
evidence_result.evidence_span: The crossover concentrations span more than two orders of magnitude, from 0.01 ppm (La at CoCrFeMn/Al2O3) to 2.76 ppm (Ti at CoCrFeNi/Cr2O3).

evidence_result.content: All multicomponent HEA crossover concentrations are below 3 ppm, mostly below 1 ppm.
evidence_result.evidence_span: First, all crossover concentrations for multicomponent HEAs are below 3 ppm at both interfaces, with the majority below 1 ppm.

evidence_result.content: CoCrFeMn has the lowest crossover concentrations across all REs at Cr2O3.
evidence_result.evidence_span: Second, CoCrFeMn consistently exhibits the lowest crossovers across all REs: 0.07 ppm Hf, 0.08 ppm Y, and 0.11 ppm Zr at Cr2O3, approximately 6× lower than the corresponding CoCrFeNi values.

evidence_result.evidence_span: Third, the oxide-dependent RE ranking from Section 3.3 manifests clearly. At Cr2O3, Hf requires the lowest concentration in most families. At Al2O3, La dominates with values as low as 0.02 ppm in CoCrFeMnNi.

evidence_result.content: CoCrFeNi + Ti is the hardest case because CoCrFeNi has strongest sulfur segregation and Ti is the weakest RE.
evidence_result.evidence_span: CoCrFeNi + Ti represents the hardest combination because CoCrFeNi has the strongest S segregation (−0.46 eV) and Ti is the weakest RE.

evidence_result.content: In CoCrFeMn/Cr2O3 + Hf, 1 ppm Hf gives >95% coverage and suppresses sulfur below 1% at 1373 K.
evidence_result.evidence_span: In CoCrFeMn/Cr2O3 + Hf (Fig. 6a), 1 ppm Hf achieves >95% coverage at 1373 K while S coverage drops to <1%.

evidence_result.content: At Al2O3, CoCrFeMn + La displaces sulfur at even lower concentration than Hf at chromia.
evidence_result.evidence_span: At Al2O3 (Fig. 6b), CoCrFeMn + La achieves complete S displacement at even lower RE concentrations (c∗= 0.007 ppm), reflecting the oxide-dependent ranking inversion where La surpasses Hf at alumina interfaces.

evidence_result.content: In the hardest CoCrFeNi + Ti cases, crossover is about 2.8 ppm.
evidence_result.evidence_span: In the hardest cases (Figs. 6c,d), CoCrFeNi paired with Ti (the weakest RE) at both oxides, the crossover shifts to ∼2.8 ppm.

evidence_result.content: Even the least favorable combination is protectable: under 3 ppm Ti gives majority coverage at 1373 K.
evidence_result.evidence_span: Nevertheless, even in this least favorable combination, <3 ppm Ti achieves majority coverage at 1373 K, confirming that the reactive element effect operates effectively across all multicomponent HEAs in this family.

evidence_result.content: At Cr2O3 in the Cantor alloy, Hf stays below 1 ppm up to about 1500 K, while Ti exceeds 1 ppm near 1100 K.
evidence_result.evidence_span: At Cr2O3 (Fig. 7a), Hf remains below 1 ppm up to ∼1500 K, while Ti crosses the 1 ppm threshold at ∼1100 K.

evidence_result.content: At Al2O3 in the Cantor alloy, La keeps sub-ppm crossover up to about 1400 K.
evidence_result.evidence_span: At Al2O3 (Fig. 7b), La maintains sub-ppm thresholds up to ∼1400 K, providing the broadest temperature window.

evidence_result.content: Example protection window: 10 ppm Hf protects the Cantor alloy at Cr2O3 up to about 1600 K.
evidence_result.evidence_span: For example, 10 ppm Hf in the Cantor alloy provides thermodynamic protection at Cr2O3 up to approximately 1600 K

evidence_result.content: At 10 ppm, even Ti can protect up to about 1300 K for moderate-temperature applications.
evidence_result.evidence_span: The curves also reveal that Ti, while the weakest RE by segregation enthalpy, can still provide protection up to ∼1300 K at 10 ppm, which may be sufficient for moderate-temperature applications where Ti is preferred for other metallurgical reasons.

evidence_result.content: At 100 ppm, all five REs nearly saturate the interface below about 1000 K.
evidence_result.evidence_span: At 100 ppm, all five REs achieve near-saturation coverage below ∼1000 K at both interfaces.

evidence_result.content: Desegregation spans roughly 400–600 K, with Hf best at chromia and La best at alumina at higher temperatures.
evidence_result.evidence_span: The desegregation transition occurs over a range of ∼400–600 K, with Hf maintaining the highest coverage at elevated temperatures at Cr2O3 and La at Al2O3, consistent with the ranking inversion.

evidence_result.content: At 1373 K, RE coverages at Cr2O3 range from 20% for Ti to 55% for Hf.
evidence_result.evidence_span: At 1373 K, RE coverages range from 20% (Ti) to 55% (Hf) at Cr2O3

evidence_result.content: At Cr2O3, adhesion rises by about 0.3 J/m2 as Cr increases from 10 to 35 at%.
evidence_result.evidence_span: Wsep at Cr2O3 increases monotonically with Cr content, with increasing Cr from 10 to 35 at% rais- ing adhesion by approximately 0.3 J/m2.

evidence_result.content: For Al2O3, both Cr and Fe improve adhesion, and the equiatomic alloy is not optimal.
evidence_result.evidence_span: For Al2O3, both Cr and Fe contribute positively with diagonally oriented contours. The equiatomic composition does not coincide with the adhesion maximum at either interface

evidence_result.content: Adhesion enhancement ordering differs from segregation ordering: Hf gives the largest ΔWsep at Cr2O3, then Zr, while Y segregates nearly as strongly as Hf.
evidence_result.evidence_span: Hf consistently produces the largest ∆Wsep at Cr2O3, fol- lowed by Zr—an ordering that differs from the segregation ranking where Y is nearly equal to Hf.

evidence_result.content: The effectiveness index shows oxide-dependent ranking inversion, with Hf first across most families and η often well above 1.
evidence_result.evidence_span: Figure 11 confirms the oxide-dependent inversion in a single dimension- less metric. At both interfaces, Hf ranks first across most families, with η values exceeding 5 in CoCrFeNi to nearly 50 in AlCoCrMnNi

evidence_result.content: Several Mn-containing alloys show negligible or repulsive sulfur segregation at Cr2O3.
evidence_result.evidence_span: Several Mn-containing alloys exhibit negligible or repulsive S segregation at Cr2O3.

evidence_result.content: Dehury et al. found no elemental segregation without oxygen, but continuous Mn surface migration and poorly adhering oxides in oxidizing atmospheres.
evidence_result.evidence_span: in the absence of oxygen, no elemental segregation was observed. In oxidizing atmospheres, however, Mn migrates continuously to the surface and forms poorly adher- ing oxide phases.

evidence_result.content: RE segregation enthalpies decrease only modestly with Mn content, by about 5–10% from 0 to 30 at% Mn.
evidence_result.evidence_span: Importantly, the RE segregation enthalpies decrease only modestly with Mn content (5–10% reduction from 0 to 30 at% Mn)

evidence_result.content: The sulfur-immunity boundary is where sulfur segregation becomes repulsive.
evidence_result.evidence_span: The contour ∆HS seg = 0 defines the thermodynamic boundary above which S segregation becomes repulsive and the alloy is inherently immune to S-induced adhesion loss without any RE addition.

evidence_result.content: The immunity boundary is approximately Al + Mn ≥25 at% at Cr2O3 and ≥30 at% at Al2O3.
evidence_result.evidence_span: The immunity boundary follows an approximate diagonal: Al + Mn ≳25 at% at Cr2O3 and ≳30 at% at Al2O3.

evidence_result.content: CoCrFeNi is deep in the sulfur-vulnerable regime, the Cantor alloy is near but below immunity, AlCoCrFeNi is near the boundary, and AlCoCrFeMnNi is on the cusp at Cr2O3.
evidence_result.evidence_span: CoCrFeNi sits deep in the S-vulnerable zone (∆HS seg = −0.46 eV at Cr2O3), explaining why RE additions are critical for this system. The Cantor alloy (20% Mn) approaches immunity but remains vulnerable. AlCoCrFeNi (20% Al) lies near the boundary, consistent with its experimentally observed moderate S sensitivity. The senary AlCoCrFeMnNi is positioned on the cusp of immunity at Cr2O3.

evidence_result.content: The predicted master-curve collapse is observed with R2 = 1.000.
evidence_result.evidence_span: Figure 14 con- firms this prediction: all data points fall on the exponential master curve c∗= cS exp(∆∆H/kBT) with R2 = 1.000.

evidence_result.evidence_span: The optimal S-immune composition for Cr2O3 is approximately Co16Cr16Fe16Ni16Al35 (at%), with Wsep = 5.95 J/m2

evidence_result.evidence_span: For Al2O3, the optimal is similar (Co17Cr17Fe17Ni17Al34, Wsep = 5.30 J/m2), offering dual-interface protection.

constraint.content: Pairwise-additivity from binary-derived Miedema enthalpies may break down in concentrated multicomponent alloys with higher-order interactions.
constraint.evidence_span: The Miedema interaction enthalpies are derived from binary systems and applied here under a pairwise additivity assumption, which has been validated for surface energy predictions in ternary and quaternary alloys [31], but may deviate in concentrated multicomponent environments where higher-order interactions become significant.

constraint.content: The McLean isotherm assumes dilute segregation and may be inaccurate at high coverages and low temperatures.
constraint.evidence_span: The McLean isotherm assumes dilute segregation, which is appropriate for trace RE and S additions but may be inaccurate at the high coverages predicted at low temperatures.

constraint.content: The model assumes an atomically sharp interface with fixed stoichiometric oxide surface compositions, neglecting real graded and defected scales.
constraint.evidence_span: The model treats the interface as atomically sharp and uses fixed stoichiometric oxide surface compositions (Cr:O = 0.4:0.6; Al:O = 0.4:0.6), neglecting the graded composition profiles and non-stoichiometric defects present in real oxide scales [9, 11].

constraint.content: The oxide is modeled as a pseudo-alloy, which overestimates oxide surface energy.
constraint.evidence_span: Additionally, the MAM computes oxide surface energies by treating the oxide as a pseudo-alloy of its metallic and non-metallic constituents, which overestimates γoxide relative to experimental values.

constraint.content: Reactive-element candidates were limited to those with literature relevance and complete Miedema parameter sets.
constraint.evidence_span: Five RE candidates comprising Hf, Y, Zr, La, and Ti were chosen based on available literature, industrial relevance and the availability of complete Miedema parameter sets [31, 34].

constraint.content: Predictions provide a thermodynamic lower bound below which kinetic optimization cannot keep the interface clean.
constraint.evidence_span: The present predictions provide the thermodynamic lower bound, below which no amount of kinetic optimization can maintain a clean interface.

constraint.content: At 35 at% Al, the alloy would likely become BCC/B2 rather than the single-phase FCC Cantor structure.
constraint.evidence_span: At 35 at% Al, the al- loy would likely adopt a BCC or B2 structure rather than the single-phase FCC that characterizes the Cantor family.

constraint.content: Although the adhesion analysis is structure-independent, practical use must consider mechanical trade-offs from phase changes.
constraint.evidence_span: While the present thermodynamic adhesion analysis is independent of crystal structure, practical implementation requires con- sideration of the associated mechanical property trade-offs.

contradiction.content: The oxide-dependent inversion was not previously reported and opposes the common practice of using a single RE across different oxide systems.
contradiction.evidence_span: This oxide-dependent inversion has not been previously reported and has direct design implications: Hf should be preferred for chromia-forming alloys, while La or Y should be preferred for alumina-forming compositions. The finding challenges the common practice of applying a single RE across different oxide-forming systems without regard for oxide chemistry.

Despite decades of research, RE selection for a given alloy–oxide combination remains largely empirical.

problem_motivation.content: Understanding and predicting oxide-scale adhesion in high-entropy alloys is a central deployment challenge because protective-scale integrity limits long-term performance.
evidence_spans: Understanding and predicting the adhesion of oxide scales to HEA substrates is therefore a central challenge for the deployment of these materials.

evidence_spans: With six principal elements, five RE candidates, two oxide types, and continuous composition ranges, the design space is inaccessible to exhaustive experimental exploration.

problem_motivation.content: The observation that some Al- and Mn-containing alloys show near-zero or positive sulfur segregation enthalpies motivates constructing a sulfur-immunity phase diagram.
evidence_spans: The observation that certain Al- and Mn-containing alloys exhibit near- zero or positive S segregation enthalpies motivates the construction of a sulfur immunity phase diagram.

prior_approach.content: Prior experimental studies established oxidation behavior in CoCrFeMnNi-based and related HEAs: in the Cantor alloy, Laplanche et al. showed Mn-rich oxides dominate and oxidation is controlled by Mn diffusion through the oxide; they also reported scale spallation during isothermal oxidation. Dehury et al. extended this to long-term 1000°C exposures, showing Mn-free CoCrFeNi forms a more continuous, adherent oxide with a much lower oxidation rate than CoCrFeMnNi, while Cr-free CoFeMnNi undergoes catastrophic oxidation; they also used vacuum annealing to show Mn surface migration is oxidation-driven rather than purely thermal. Holcomb et al. further confirmed across CoCrFeMnNi variants that low-Mn, high-Cr compositions have the best scale retention.
evidence_spans: Extensive experimental work has established the oxidation phenomenology of key HEA families.

For the CoCrFeMnNi (Cantor) system, Laplanche et al. [9] showed that Mn-rich oxides (α-Mn2O3 at 600–800◦C, Mn3O4 at 900◦C) dominate the scale, with an oxidation activation energy of 130 ± 10 kJ/mol controlled by Mn diffusion through the oxide rather than sluggish diffusion in the alloy matrix [10].
Laplanche et al. [9] reported scale spallation during isothermal oxidation of the Cantor alloy, manifested as small weight losses in TGA curves.

Dehury et al. [11] extended these observations to 30-day exposures at 1000◦C, demonstrating that Mn-free CoCrFeNi forms a more continuous, better-adherent oxide with an oxidation rate constant one order of magnitude lower than that of the Cantor alloy, while Cr-free CoFeMnNi undergoes catastrophic oxidation with phase decomposition.

More directly, Dehury et al. [11] found that after 30 days at 1000◦C, CoCrFeNi formed a relatively continuous oxide layer with good surface adherence, whereas CoCrFeMnNi exhibited a rough, discontinuous, and significantly spalled scale with Kirkendall pores at the metal–oxide interface.

Dehury et al. [11] provided direct experimental evidence for this duality. Their vacuum-annealing experiment at 1000◦C confirmed that Mn migration to the surface is oxidation-driven rather than thermally driven
Holcomb et al. [7] confirmed this hierarchy across eight CoCrFeMnNi variants, finding that low-Mn, high-Cr compositions exhibited the best scale retention.

prior_approach.content: Prior studies on alloy design for oxidation resistance showed that Al and Cr are key for forming protective oxides, whereas Mn is detrimental; Butler and Weaver found that sufficiently high Al additions (≥20 at%) promote continuous protective Al2O3, and Lu et al. showed that minor Y/Hf co-doping in AlCoCrFeNi yields a thin, uniform α-Al2O3 scale. Reviews further concluded that AlCoCrFeNi alloys, especially with refractory additions, are among the most promising oxidation-resistant HEAs.
evidence_spans: For Al-containing systems, Butler and Weaver [12] showed that ≥20 at% Al promotes continuous protective Al2O3
while Lu et al. [4] demonstrated that co-doping AlCoCrFeNi with only 0.02 at% each of Y and Hf produces a uniform α-Al2O3 scale just 4.6 µm thick after 1000 h at 1100◦C.
Lu et al. [4] achieved exceptional oxidation resistance in Y/Hf co-doped AlCoCrFeNi, an alumina-forming alloy

Comprehensive reviews [13] have concluded that Al and Cr are the most important elements for protective oxide formation, while Mn degrades oxidation resistance through porous, poorly adhering scale phases.
The review by Veselkov et al. [13] concluded that AlCoCrFeNi alloys with additions of refractory elements represent the most promising direction for oxidation-resistant HEAs

prior_approach.content: Prior work documented sulfur-induced oxide-scale adhesion loss in Ni-based superalloys and increasingly also in HEAs.
evidence_spans: as documented in Ni-based superalloys [18, 19] and increasingly in HEA systems [5, 7].

evidence_spans: Chen et al. [24] further demonstrated that selective oxidation of Cr, Co, and Fe in Al0.1CrCoFeNi creates a Ni-enriched subsurface layer that hinders repassivation

prior_approach.content: Prior computational work used first-principles DFT to study specific alloy systems, and the authors previously extended the macroscopic atom model (MAM) to multicomponent alloys, validating it against DFT for CoCrFeNi and AlCoCrFeNi. Their previous DFT work also found that Ni sites are the least favorable for rare-earth segregation, underscoring composition effects on segregation tendency.

In our previous paper [29], we extended the macroscopic atom model (MAM) [30, 31] to multicomponent alloys, where we validated the framework against DFT for CoCrFeNi and AlCoCrFeNi systems.
Moreover, in our previous work, DFT calculations demonstrated that Ni sites are the most unfavorable for REs to segregate, further highlighting the effect of composition on segregation tendency [25].

inspiration_source.content: The interpretation of the Cr-adhesion trend is inspired by analogy to the percolation-threshold concept for passive-film formation reported by Xie et al., specifically that a minimum of about 10–12 at% Cr is required for continuous passive film formation in Fe–Cr and Ni–Cr systems.
evidence_spans: The dominance of Cr as the adhesion lever at Cr2O3 connects to the percolation threshold concept. Xie et al. [41] showed that a minimum of ∼10–12 at% Cr is required for continuous passive film formation in Fe–Cr and Ni–Cr systems.

causal_claim.content: The oxide-dependent ranking inversion among reactive elements is caused by the interplay between RE–oxygen and RE–matrix interaction enthalpies; specifically, La outranks Hf at Al2O3 because La interacts more strongly with the Al-dominated oxide, whereas the reverse holds at Cr2O3, and La’s mismatch penalty is too small to overturn its Al2O3 advantage.
evidence_spans: The screening reveals an oxide-dependent ranking inversion, with Hf dominating at Cr2O3 and La dominating at Al2O3, driven by the interplay between RE–O and RE–matrix interaction enthalpies.

The inversion originates in Term 1: La’s interaction with the Al-dominated oxide (−1.52 eV) exceeds that of Hf (−1.38 eV) at Al2O3, driven by the more exothermic La–Al interaction (∆H◦ LaAl = −231 kJ/mol vs. Hf–Al: −215 kJ/mol), while the reverse holds at Cr2O3 (∆H◦ LaCr = +93 kJ/mol).
The mismatch penalty for La (Term 4: +0.24 eV) is constant across oxide types and insufficient to reverse the ranking at Al2O3.

causal_claim.content: Segregation enthalpy difference is the single thermodynamic parameter governing the universal exponential collapse of RE/S crossover concentrations, so knowing RE and S segregation enthalpies allows designers to read off the minimum RE concentration from the universal curve.
evidence_spans: All crossover concentrations collapse onto a universal exponential governed by the segregation enthalpy difference, providing a transferable design rule.
The entire complexity of alloy composition, RE choice, and oxide type reduces to a single thermodynamic parameter.

The practical consequence is that an alloy designer who knows ∆HRE seg and ∆HS seg for any system obtainable from a seconds-long MAM calculation can read the minimum RE concentration directly from the universal curve.

evidence_spans: demonstrating that Mn-free CoCrFeNi forms a more continuous, better-adherent oxide with an oxidation rate constant one order of magnitude lower than that of the Cantor alloy

causal_claim.content: Al-containing alloys have lower surface energies because Al has a lower surface enthalpy than the other constituent elements; Mn also lowers surface energy relative to CoCrFeNi because Mn has a comparatively low surface enthalpy.
evidence_spans: Al-containing alloys consistently exhibit lower surface energies by 0.2–0.3 J/m2, reflecting the low surface enthalpy of Al (76 kJ/mol) compared to Co (127), Cr (121), Fe (129), Ni (121), and Mn (85 kJ/mol) [31].

evidence_spans: Because the alloy surface energy enters both the numerator of Wsep and the interfacial energy term with partially canceling contributions, the cross-interface chemical interactions, rather than the surface energies themselves, emerge as the dominant factor differentiating adhesion across families

causal_claim.content: All alloy families lose adhesion monotonically as sulfur concentration rises, but their sulfur sensitivity depends on composition; Al-containing alloys are less sulfur-sensitive because sulfur segregates more weakly, so less sulfur reaches the interface and disrupts fewer bonds.
evidence_spans: All families show monotonic adhesion decline with increasing S concentration, but the rate and magnitude of decline differ substantially.

This reduced sensitivity of Al-containing alloys correlates with their weaker S segregation enthalpies: less S reaches the interface at equilibrium, and the interfacial bonding network is less disrupted per unit of S coverage.

causal_claim.content: Although CoCrFeMn is highly sulfur-sensitive in principle, it requires very little RE for protection because its strong Mn–S bulk interaction weakens sulfur segregation while Hf still segregates strongly, giving the lowest RE/S crossover concentrations.

causal_claim.content: Practical RE additions exceed thermodynamic minimum concentrations by 2–3 orders of magnitude because extra RE is needed to overcome kinetic limitations, internal oxidation, and sequestration at grain boundaries.

The excess serves primarily to compensate for kinetic limitations including slow bulk diffusion of RE to the interface, consumption by internal oxidation, and RE sequestration at grain boundaries [14, 15].

constraint.content: The model’s thermodynamic treatment has several validity limits: Miedema interaction enthalpies are binary-derived and used with a pairwise-additivity assumption that may break down in concentrated multicomponent alloys where higher-order interactions matter; the McLean isotherm assumes dilute segregation and may become inaccurate at the high coverages predicted at low temperatures.
evidence_spans: The Miedema interaction enthalpies are derived from binary systems and applied here under a pairwise additivity assumption, which has been validated for surface energy predictions in ternary and quaternary alloys [31], but may deviate in concentrated multicomponent environments where higher-order interactions become significant.
